No distinctive vocabulary, no recoverable context.

The machine's only candidate here, and the phrase is real — “good old age” occurs in exactly four KJV verses. But Gideon is the wrong one of the four. Judges 8:32 is a death notice whose sequel is Judges 8:33-9:5: the nation goes whoring after Baalberith as soon as Gideon is dead, and Abimelech kills seventy brothers on one stone to take the succession. Ether 10:16-17 is the opposite in every particular — the father anoints his successor himself, and the successor 'did that which was good in the sight of the Lord, all his days'. 1 Chronicles 29:28, David's death notice, is the King James verse that holds a good old age and an orderly royal succession in one sentence, and the link at 10:16 is written there.

“the whole face of the” is a KJV singleton, which is why it ranked, and the singleton is a mist. Genesis 2:6 is the vapour that went up from the earth and watered the whole face of the ground before there was rain or a man to till it — an image of emptiness before habitation. Ether 10:21 is the same phrase used for the reverse: 'the whole face of the land northward was covered with inhabitants'. The word after the shared run differs too ('ground' against 'land'), and the Book of Mormon's 'whole face of the land' is one of its own recurrent formulae. A singleton whose sense inverts and whose next word diverges is not a source.

This is the typological pull of the whole chapter and the wording will not bear it, which makes it the entry most worth writing. Ether 10 is a king-list about taxation, corvée, prisons and rebellion; 1 Samuel 8:11-18 is the King James Bible's set-piece on what a king will do to a people, and Ether 6:19-23 has already borrowed its opening move (1 Samuel 8:5, the demand for a king), so the source is demonstrably in this record's hands. 1 Samuel 8:12 even runs agriculture into armament in the order Ether 10:25-27 does — 'to ear his ground, and to reap his harvest, and to make his instruments of war'. But the only shared content word is 'reap'; Ether has 'weapons of war', which occurs in nine KJV verses, and not 'instruments of war', which occurs in three and is 1 Samuel's phrase. And the sense is inverted at the point that matters: 1 Samuel 8 is about a king conscripting his subjects' labour, whereas the subject of Ether 10:25-27 is the people themselves, in the reign the chapter calls the most blessed and prosperous it knows. The Samuel material governs 10:5-10, where the taxes and the prisons are; it does not govern the prosperity catalogue. Recorded so that a reader who sees the type is told the catalogue saw it and declined it.

The second half of the same temptation. Ether 10:25-27 moves in three verses from tools 'both to plough and to sow, to reap and to hoe' to 'all manner of weapons of war', which is the direction of Joel 3:10 ('Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruninghooks into spears') and the reverse of Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3. There is no verbal contact at all: the King James word in all three verses is 'plowshares', a noun, and Ether's is 'plough', a verb, and no other term is shared. The sequence is also an artifact of the list's own logic — a catalogue of manufactures that runs from farming to cloth to tools to weapons is ordered by subject matter, not by allusion. Filed rather than passed over in silence because the swords-and-ploughshares figure is the first thing a reader of these three verses is likely to reach for.

“weapons of war” occurs in nine KJV verses spread across Deuteronomy, Judges, 2 Samuel, Ecclesiastes, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, which is too wide a distribution to point at any one of them, and Ezekiel 32:27 — the uncircumcised mighty gone down to hell with their weapons of war, their swords under their heads — has nothing else in common with a manufacturing inventory. The genuine borrowing in this verse is the other half of it, 'all manner of work of exceeding curious workmanship', which is Bezaleel's vocabulary from Exodus 35:32-35 and is adjudicated at 10:23 with 10:27 in its recurrenceRefs.

'They were in a land that was choice above all lands, for the Lord had spoken it.' Jeremiah 2:2 supplies only the five-word connective 'in a land that was' and then reads 'not sown', of the wilderness Israel followed God through — the opposite kind of land in the opposite kind of sentence. The Book of Mormon's phrase here is its own: 'choice above all lands' and 'choice above all other lands' occur nowhere in the King James Bible and repeatedly in this record, from 1 Nephi 2:20 through Ether 1:38, 2:7, 2:10 and 9:20. What is King James in Ether 10:28 is the promised-land material behind it, and that is adjudicated at 10:23 against Deuteronomy 8:7-9, with 10:28 in its recurrenceRefs.

“forty and two years” is a KJV singleton — 2 Chronicles 22:2, Ahaziah's age at accession — and it is rejected on the arithmetic. Ether 10 uses the number three times, at 10:8 (Riplakish's reign), 10:15 (Levi's captivity) and 10:32 (Com's half-kingdom), for three different kings and three different kinds of period, none of them an age; a numeral a chapter reaches for three times independently is that chapter's habit and not a borrowing. 2 Chronicles 22:2 is in any case one of the King James Bible's known arithmetical cruxes, since 2 Kings 8:26 gives Ahaziah's age as twenty and two — which is a reason to be more careful with the verse, not less. The same entry covers 'the half of the kingdom' in this verse: it occurs in three KJV verses, all of them Ahasuerus offering Esther a gift (Esther 5:3, 5:6, 7:2), where the sense is a king's extravagant promise and not, as here, a usurper's seizure by war.
